text: The Yamaha DX1 is the top-tier model in Yamaha's DX series of FM synthesizers, featuring two sets of the same synthesizer chipset used in the DX7, enabling either double polyphony, split operation with two voices, or dual (layered) instrument voices. It also has double the voice memory of the DX7 and includes an independent voice bank for each of two synthesizer channels ("sound engines"). Each of the 64 performance combinations can be assigned a single voice number or a combination of two voice numbers—one from channel A and one from channel B. The DX1 is housed in a handmade Brazilian rosewood case and features a 73-key weighted wooden keyboard with polyphonic aftertouch. On the front panel's left side, a printed algorithm chart outlines the 32 selectable algorithms and their operator configurations. It uses solid push-buttons instead of membrane buttons like the DX7, with individual LEDs indicating current status. Compared to the DX5 and DX7, the DX1 has more displays, improving accessibility and programmability. The performance section includes a backlit LCD display (40 × 2 characters) that shows selected programs in Single, Dual, or Split mode, LFO settings, and other voice-specific parameters. The algorithm panel features thirteen single-character 7-segment numeric displays that indicate the selected algorithm and the position and relationships of active operators, with each display linked via stripe-style LEDs; the top display shows feedback and the bottom shows the algorithm number. The oscillator panel has two LEDs indicating frequency ratio (top) or fixed frequency (bottom) in Hz mode, one LED for positive or negative detune, a single-character numeric display (top) for detune amount, and a four-character numeric display (bottom) for the frequency value. The envelope panel includes two LEDs indicating center pitch (left) or amplitude level (right) mode, eight double-character numeric displays for envelope parameters, and four 16-segment bar-style LEDs that graphically show rates (in center pitch mode) or levels (in amplitude mode). The keyboard scaling panel has eight individual LEDs for selected curve response, three double-character numeric displays (left to right) for left depth, break point, and right depth, and one single-character numeric display for rate scaling. The sensitivity panel includes two single-character numeric displays for key velocity (top) and amplitude modulation (bottom), one double-character numeric display for output level, and one 16-segment bar-style LED for graphical output level display. During its 1985 production year, only 140 DX1 units were made, with a retail value of US $13,900 (equivalent to US$40,600 adjusted for inflation). The Yamaha DX5, introduced in 1985 with a list price of US$3,495, shares the same synth engine as the DX1 but lacks its fully weighted keys, polyphonic aftertouch, rosewood case, wooden keyboard, and user interface features such as parameter displays. It includes 76 keys, channel aftertouch, and slightly improved MIDI features. Programming on the DX1 remains slightly easier than on the DX5 due to its extensive parameter displays, though both are easier to program than the DX7 because of larger displays and dedicated programming buttons. In 2019, UVI released the FM Suite plugin bundle, which includes recreations of multiple FM synths, such as the DX1, DX21, DS-8, TQ5, FVX-1, TX81Z, DX100, and GS2. At NAMM 2025, Behringer announced the BX1, an unofficial reissue of the DX1 that adds CS-80-inspired analog filters, modern effects, and 32-voice polyphony.
